WX002-004003-:
A standing stone, identified as 'Leac Mhic Eochadha' and associated with the inauguration site of the Uí Cinsealaigh at Loggan, was located close to the motte and bailey (WX002-004001-) according to Orpen (1911, 210–11). This identification is not completely certain due to the Irish phraseology of the sources. However, the stone was still being used as an assembly point as late as 1592 when landholders from areas in the Kinsellaghs (just north of Gorey), Kilcheele (Mac Vadock’s Country) just west of Gorey in which Leac Mhic Eochaidh itself lay), and the Macamores (east and south of Gorey – modern-day Ballaghkeen North) met here with the Lord Deputy Henry Sidney to seek title deeds under English law (pers. com. Conchubhar Ó Crualaoich). Many of those involved had already done this at early dates. Cist burials (WX002-004002-) were discovered nearby. The location of the stone is not known exactly and it does not survive, but it appears to have been S of the bailey (Westropp 1904, 321).
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wexford' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1996). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of revision: 18 August 2017

The location is marked on a field map of the Geological Survey of Ireland at a point on the N-facing slope of a col between hills c. 400m to the E and W that are c. 40-50m higher than the col. The steep slope is strewn with boulders in rough pasture, but there is no evidence that there was ever a structure here.

WX007-076007-:
This site was excavated (E3502) during 2005 as a part of a complex area know as Site 42-44 of the N11 Gorey to Arklow link. An extensive area (dims. 250m N-S 48-60m E-W) across the road-take was excavated, but geophysical survey indicates that activity extended outside this to the E, W and SW. Situated on the lower NW-facing slope of Ask Hill.
This is at the extreme NW part of the excavated area. A feldspathic tuff stone with a rectangular cross-section (dims. c. 0.75m x c. 0.5m; H 1m) was excavated and found to have been prised from an underlying glacial erratic and wedged upright with waste from a dressing with iron tools. (Stevens 2008a, 392-3; 2008, 44-6)
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload: 16 March, 2012

WX023-001----:
Described as ‘Ramshaghroe’ on the 1839 and 1924 eds of the OS 6-inch map, it is located on a shoulder of fairly high ground at the SW end of the Blackstairs Mountains. The SE-NW Aughnacrew River is c. 450m to the SW with Ballyleigh Hill beyond it. There are extensive views of Mount Brandon and the valley of the N-S River Barrow to the NW. A reference from an 18th century dictionary by O'Reilly (pers. Com. Conchubhar Ó Crualaoich) describes Raimseach ruadh, the wife of the Gobán Saer, as one of two stones which St. Moling had metamorphosed, the other being her companion, but a second stone has never been identified. A local blacksmith attempted to destroy the larger stone through three charges inserted in the stone, but when these holes bled the attempt was abandoned. This is a granite stone with quartz veins and a sub-rectangular cross-section at the base (dims. 0.35-0.85m x 0.65m; H 1.9m) aligned generally ESE-WNW. For O'Reilly's dictionary see this web-page accessed on 9 July, 2014 https://archive.org/stream/irishenglishdict00ore#page/688/mode/2up
The above description is derived from the published 'Archaeological Inventory of County Wexford' (Dublin: Stationery Office, 1996). In certain instances the entries have been revised and updated in the light of recent research.
Compiled by: Michael Moore
Date of upload/revision: 25 June, 2012
